root.note: Wiktionary takes patata straight from Taíno batata. The RAE, as Wiktionary reports it, calls it a blend of papa + batata. Both accounts include batata.

history: Patata is what happens when two American plants get mixed up. Spaniards found the sweet potato in the Caribbean, where Taíno speakers called it batata, and later found the potato in Peru, where Quechua speakers called it papa. Europe confused the two. The RAE's dictionary from 1737 to 1803 still defines patata as the same as batata, and only in 1817 links it to the plant we mean today. Why Spain moved to patata is debated, and French influence is one suggestion. Latin America and the Canaries still say papa. Andalusia does too. So in Spain's shops ask for patatas, but expect papas in Gran Canaria or Buenos Aires.
historyEinfach: Spanish speakers found two plants in America. One was the sweet potato. People in the Caribbean called it batata. The other was the potato. People in Peru called it papa. In Europe, people mixed up the two names, and patata was the result. In Latin America, people still say papa. In most of Spain, people say patata.

elsewhere.text: English took the word from Spanish, so it inherited the same mix-up.
Portuguese uses the Taíno word, batata, for the potato itself.
German took another route: Kartoffel comes from Italian tartufoli.
French made its own name: an apple of the earth.
